documentation.range:
The Monarch Butterfly, Danaus plexippus, is primarily distributed throughout the Americas, from southern Canada, through the United States, Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America, to South America, north of the Amazon Basin (Opler and Wright 1999). In North America, this species undergoes an iconic annual migration. Every year, millions of Monarch Butterflies travel from overwintering sites in Central Mexico and coastal California, to summer breeding grounds throughout the United States and Canada (Urquhart and Urquhart 1978). By the late summer and fall, after several generations, individuals embark on the return journey, travelling distances up to 4,000 km (Brower 1996). However, in much of its neotropical range within the Americas and elsewhere, this species does not participate in continental scale migrations and can be found year-round as a resident (Opler and Wright 1999). Some short distance seasonal migrations, from lowlands to highlands or coastal to inland areas, often still take place in these regions (Zhan et al. 2014).

Monarchs are also found in many other parts of the world, including Europe (mostly southern Spain, Portugal, the Azores and the Canary Islands), Australia, New Zealand, many Pacific Islands, including Hawai‘i, Taiwan and the Philippines (Opler and Wright 1999, Neves et al. 2001, Smith et al. 2005). In most cases, it is thought that occasional visitors or vagrants, often blown in by big weather events, eventually became established (Clarke and Zalucki 2004). There are now breeding populations in many of these regions (Neves et al. 2001, Zalucki and Clarke 2004). In the countries of occurrence table for this assessment, these populations are listed as "native" as the species reached these areas naturally. However, the Monarch is generally considered native only in the Americas and the Caribbean, because the host plants utilized elsewhere are non-native, having been introduced in the last several hundred years (Fernández-Haeger et al. 2015, Buden and Tennent 2017). These more recently established populations are not likely to be viable if the non-native host plants are eradicated in these areas. For these reasons, these populations are excluded from the Red List assessment.

The estimated extent of occurrence for this species (including only the resident population in the Americas and the overwintering regions of the migratory subspecies) is at least 17 million km². This species is too widespread to get an accurate estimated area of occupancy (AOO).

There are at least two subspecies of Danaus plexippus currently recognized: D. p. plexippus is the migratory subspecies found in the United States, Canada, Mexico, the Canary Islands, Madeira, the Azores, Bermuda and numerous Pacific islands including Hawai‘i, Australia and New Zealand; D. p. megalippe is the non-migratory subspecies found in southern Florida and throughout the Caribbean, Central America, and South America north of the Amazon Drainage (Smith et al. 2005). Pelham (2008) recognizes several colour varieties of D. p. megalippe, including portoricensis, leucogyne, and tobagi, as additional subspecies.
documentation.population:
Due to yearly monitoring of the migratory subspecies (Danaus plexippus plexippus) at over wintering sites in California and Mexico, current population estimates for a portion of the population are available. During the 2020–2021 winter season, surveys found monarchs occupying 2.10 hectares of forest in Mexico (World Wildlife Fund Mexico 2021). While the estimated number of Monarchs per hectare varies from 6.9 to 60.9 million (Calvert 2015), 21.1 million is widely used as a best estimate (Thogmartin et al. 2017a). Therefore, there were an estimated 44 million butterflies at overwintering sites in Mexico during the 2020–2021 season. During the same season in California, surveys documented only 1,914 butterflies (Xerces Society Western Monarch Thanksgiving Count 2021). The counts for the western migratory population have never been so low, and experts have suggested that the migration is vulnerable to collapse once population size dips below the threshold of 30,000 individuals (Schultz et al. 2017). Despite reliable data for the migratory subspecies, total population size estimates are unknown for D. plexippus at the species level, because there is little population data available for the non-migratory subspecies D. p. megalippe, which occupies a substantial portion of the total range from the Caribbean south, through Central America, to northern portions of South America.

Long term declines for both eastern and western migratory populations of the subspecies D. p. plexippus have been reported (Brower et al. 2011, Semmens et al. 2016, Schultz et al. 2017). The most pronounced declines for the eastern migratory population were seen from 1996 to 2014, when the population declined by 84% (Semmens et al. 2016). In the last 10 years, declines have slowed, and the population has stabilized around 55 million individuals, with butterflies occupying an average of 2.59 ha each winter. However, Semmens et al. (2016) suggest 6 ha of occupied forest is needed to maintain a resilient eastern migratory population. Though the population may appear stable, below 6 ha of occupied forest, overwintering colonies may not be large enough to maintain the appropriate microhabitat conditions to prevent from freezing (Semmens et al. 2016). Due to these factors, this population has a quasi-extinction risk of 5–43% over the next 20 years (Semmens et al. 2016). For the western migratory population, an estimated population size of 3 to 10 million in the 1980s, has declined to less than 1,914 individuals in the winter season of 2020–2021, a decline of 99.9% (Pelton and Knight 2021, Xerces Society Western Monarch Thanksgiving Count 2021). Based on log-scale geometric growth models developed by Schultz et al. (2017) and modified by Voorhies et al. (2019) to include additional data from 2016 to 2019, estimated annual population growth for the western migratory population is 0.839. Based on this current growth rate and a quasi-extinction threshold ranging from 20,000 to 50,000 individuals, Voorhies et al. (2019) suggest a 99.99% risk of quasi-extinction over 50 years. Individuals outside the naturally native range were not taken into account for this analysis.

Where this species is non-migratory, the population trend is not known with certainty, although it is thought to be stable (NatureServe 2020). As mentioned, it is unknown what percentage of the total population the migratory individuals represent. Therefore, total population declines cannot be estimated, and the extinction risk is unknown. However, it is unlikely that declines are over the 30% threshold for classification as Vulnerable. It is also likely that this species would remain at low risk of extinction even if the North American migratory phenomena collapsed.
documentation.habitats:
Monarchs prefer open habitats including native prairies, weedy fields, meadows, marshes and roadsides (Opler and Wright 1999). This species is seldom found in heavily forested areas, mountains, or desert regions (Center for Biological Diversity et al. 2014, Brock 2008). Males are often seen patrolling open fields to search for females during the breeding season (Opler and Wright 1999). Adults feed on the flowers of their larval host plant, milkweed (Asclepias spp.), as well as many other types of flowers, especially composites (Family: Asteraceae) (Opler and Wright 1999, Brock 2008). Like other milkweed butterflies (species in the Danaus genus), Monarch larvae feed on milkweeds (Asclepias spp.) and other plants in the Apocynaceae family (Opler and Wright 1999, Brock 2008). Larvae sequester cardenolide secondary compounds contained within the milkweed sap, making them distasteful to predators as larvae and adults (Jones and Agrawal 2016).

Monarchs in the North American migratory subspecies overwinter in large colonies within Oyamel Fir (Abies religiosa) forests of central Mexico (Brower et al. 2004, Vidal and Rendón-Salinas 2014) or forested groves along the coast of California. In the spring, the butterflies come out of reproductive diapause and mate before dispersing (Jepsen et al. 2015). From Mexico, butterflies head north, reaching southern Canada and the northeastern United States by midsummer (Malcom et al. 1993). From coastal California, monarchs disperse northward and eastward, eventually reaching interior parts of the West including Nevada, Idaho, Oregon, Washington, Utah, Arizona (Dingle et al. 2005, Jepsen et al. 2015), and probably other areas west of the Rocky Mountains, including as far north as southern British Columbia (Pyle 2015).
documentation.threats:
Where declines in the migratory sub-species have been observed, the main threats are degradation of breeding habitat, loss of overwintering habitat, and climate change associated increases in severe weather events (The Center for Biological Diversity et al. 2014, Shahani et al. 2015, Crone et al. 2019). Threats to the non-migratory subspecies are not documented, but outside the core range within North America, threats appear to be minimal.

For the migratory subspecies, the main threat in summer breeding areas is increased agricultural intensification and associated declines in milkweed host plants and nectar sources (Pleasants and Oberhauser 2013, Flockhart et al. 2015). For example, in the Upper Midwest region, Pleasants and Oberhauser (2012) found milkweed had declined by as much as 58% from 1999 to 2010. Milkweed losses have recently been exacerbated by an increased use of glyphosate herbicides within croplands, resulting from expanded use of herbicide resistant genetically modified (GM) corn and soybean crops (Pleasants and Oberhauser 2012, Flockhart et al. 2015). Other threats to milkweed include aggressive management of rights of way and roadside vegetation in the form of mowing and herbicide spraying, urban development, urban landscaping practices, and loss of croplands (Borders and Lee-Mader 2014). At overwintering sites in both Mexico and California, habitat loss and forest fragmentation continues to be problematic (Brower et al. 2002). From 1971 to 1999, 44% of 42,020 hectares of suitable overwintering habitat in Mexico was degraded as a result of commercial logging (legal and illegal), conversion for agriculture and pastures, charcoal production, and controlled burns (Brower et al. 2002). More recently, deforestation due to logging has slowed and reserves have been established to protect this habitat (Vidal and Rendón-Salinas 2014). However, enforcing protections has not always been successful and habitats are still under pressure due to illegal logging, agriculture, urban development, grazing, fires, forest disease, water diversion for human use, and climate change (Vidal et al. 2013, Center for Biological Diversity et al. 2014, Brower et al. 2016). In California, the main driver of habitat loss is urban development and a lack of proactive management (Jepsen and Black 2015). Since 1985, at least 76 overwintering sites have been lost and many additional sites have been degraded due to wildfire, minor tree trimming or removal, drought, tree pests, and mismanagement (Sakai and Calvert 1991, Pelton et al. 2016, Pelton 2020).

Severe weather and climate change have also been suggested as threats for the migratory subspecies. Habitat suitability models predict overwintering sites in Mexico and California will become less suitable in the coming years (Fisher et al. 2018, Oberhauser and Petersen 2003). Severe weather events, which are increasing in frequency, are also problematic. For example, a particularly cold, wet storm in 2002 killed as many as 500 million butterflies (Brower et al. 2002). On the other hand, warmer temperatures may deplete lipid reserves and expedite reproductive development, leading to early departures from overwintering areas (Oberhauser and Petersen 2003). Increased incidence of drought is also likely to adversely impact monarchs. Availability of floral resources along autumn migration routes is critical to fall migration success and is positively correlated with abundance at over wintering sites in both Mexico and California (Stevens and Frey 2010, Saunders et al. 2019).

Other noted threats include parasites and pathogens and increased insecticide use. The native protozoan parasite Ophryocistis elektroscirrha (OE), which reduces fecundity in heavily infected individuals, has increased in incidence since the 1990s (Altizer 2001, Thogmartin et al. 2017b). Increased insecticide use has been implicated in declines of butterfly population in both California and the UK (Gilburn et al. 2015, Forister et al. 2016). In exposure trials conducted on Monarch larvae in the field, neonicotinoid (clothianidin) exposure caused sublethal and lethal effects, such as slower development, lower body mass, and caused higher mortality rates (Pecenka and Lundgren 2015). Neonicotinoid use in particular is concerning because its use has increased 48-fold from 2003 to 2010 in the United States (Thogmartin et al. 2017b).
documentation.measures: Many, mostly voluntary, conservation efforts are underway across North America to protect the migratory phenomena of the migratory subspecies. There are few, if any, conservation efforts in place to protect this species outside its migratory range. In Mexico, the overwintering sites have been protected, with varying levels of success, since 1975 (Center for Biological Diversity et al. 2014). Most recently, the Mexican government set aside 56,259 hectares of forest, running in a belt along the border of Michoacán and Estado Mexico, to form the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve (MBBR), which remains in place today (Vidal and Rendón-Salinas 2014). In 2008, the MBBR became a UNESCO World Heritage Site (UNESCO 2013). Canada has also taken steps to protect Monarchs, including the creation of an International Network of Monarch Butterfly Reserve, with Mexico, in 1995, and listing the Monarch as a species of special concern under the Species at Risk Act in 2003 (Vidal and Rendón-Salinas 2014, Shahani et al. 2015). In the United States, the migratory subspecies has been petitioned for protections under the Endangered Species Act (The Center for Biological Diversity et al. 2014). The US Fish and Wildlife Service (2021) recently announced that listing the monarch was “warranted but precluded by higher priority actions”. Over 85 federal and state agencies, non-governmental organizations, businesses and academic programs collaborate on monarch conservation projects, such as habitat restoration, milkweed planting, and community science data collection (Monarch Joint Venture 2020).
documentation.use_trade:
The Monarch is one of nine butterflies permitted for release across state lines by the US Department of Agriculture (Pyle 2010), except in Washington and Oregon, which have placed state limits on this practice. It is therefore often reared by commercial breeders to be sold, usually for educational or ceremonial purposes (Pyle 2010). It is also utilized by the Butterfly House Industry (BHI), which is estimated to be worth 100 million dollars (USD) a year (Boppré and Vane-Wright 2012). Some commercial operations collect a portion of their stock from wild populations (Pelton 2018), but as neither industry is regulated, it is unclear to what extent this is the case.

In Mexico, the Monarch is a tourist attraction at its overwintering sites in the Oyamel Fir forests of Michoacán and Estado Mexico (Vidal et al. 2014). There is a similar draw at some sites in coastal California, including in the communities of Pacific Grove, Pismo Beach, and Santa Cruz. It is unclear whether this eco-tourism impacts this species.
documentation.rationale:
The Monarch Butterfly (Danaus plexippus) is widely recognized for its remarkable long-distance migration. Native to the Americas, from southern Canada to northern South America, breeding populations of this species are now found around the world. These more recently established populations are excluded from the Red List assessment as they are dependent on host plant species which are non-native to these areas (see Geographic Range text).

Only the North American subspecies, D. p. plexippus, is considered migratory and there are two primary migration patterns. East of the Rocky Mountains, over several generations, butterflies migrate back and forth from overwintering sites in the Oyamel Fir forests of Central Mexico to summer breeding areas across the eastern United States and southern Canada. Similarly, in western North America, butterflies migrate from overwintering sites along the Pacific Coast to breeding areas in all U.S. states west of the Rocky Mountains. The subspecies D. p. megalippe, found in the Neotropics from Florida, through southern Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America, to northern South America, breeds year-round and does not embark on long distance migrations. As larvae, Monarch Butterflies feed almost exclusively on Milkweed (Asclepias spp.).

Long term population declines, primarily due to habitat loss in overwintering sites and host plant declines in summer breeding areas, have been observed in the migratory subspecies, D. p. plexippus. In the last 10 years, the population size appears to have stabilized, though these subpopulations remain at high risk of quasi-extinction due to stochastic events. However, where this species is non-migratory, the population size and trend are not known with certainty, though the population is thought to be stable. Due to the widespread nature of this species, overall large population size, and declines likely to be less than 30%, the risk of extinction remains low. Therefore, this species is assessed as Least Concern. However, because the migratory phenomenon is certainly at risk, conservation efforts should continue, and additional research on the non-migratory subspecies should be carried out to ensure population stability.

threats.text: The native protozoan parasite Ophryocistis elektroscirrha (OE) reduces fecundity in heavily infected individuals and renders them less fit for long-distance migrations, due to smaller wing sizes and lower mass (Altizer 2001). Incidence of this parasite is higher in non-migratory populations.
